No, it wasn't just the cold snap. 

While the colder weather did play a part, it only accounts for **$21.35** of the increase on your June bill. The real driver was a massive, sudden jump in your "always-on" background load—the power your home draws continuously, 24 hours a day, even overnight when everyone is asleep. This background load alone added **$80.31** to your bill.

Your meter shows that this change happened overnight on **Saturday, June 8**:
* **Before June 8:** Your background draw was steady, averaging about 5 to 6 units (kWh) per day.
* **From June 8 onward:** It suddenly shot up to over 17 units on that Saturday, and has remained between 16 and 17 units every single day since.

Because this extra draw is running constantly around the clock—including between 2 am and 5 am—it doesn't track the outdoor temperature. Normal heating goes up and down as the weather changes, but this is a flat, continuous line. This suggests that something was plugged in, switched on, or developed a fault on June 8 and has been running continuously ever since.
